title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu, Jianguo Li, Yu Zhang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
authors: Ayman bin Kamruddin, Christopher Lam, Gaurav Patil, Mirco Musolesi, Mario di Bernardo, Michael J. Richardson
publish: arXiv
abstract: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.

title: ZERITH V2.5: From Predictive Power to Policy Learnability
authors: Chenxi Han, Ruby, Epoch, Orion, Luke, Bin, Dusk, Lyra, Cal, Alvin, Hubert, Alex, Jiahe Han, Tao Zhang, Hang Liu, Shoujie Li, Yizhe Li, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu, Guoping Pan, Yi Cheng
publish: arXiv
abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning. We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.

title: Weak Hilbert's Nullstellensatz for skew polynomials over division rings
authors: Dinh Van Hoang, Vo Ngoc Thieu, Phan Thanh Toan
publish: arXiv
abstract: We establish a weak Nullstellensatz for skew polynomial rings $R_n=D[x_1,\ldots,x_n;σ]$, where $D$ is a division ring and the commuting variables induce the same automorphism $σ$ of $D$. For $n\ge2$, we characterize the pairs $(D,σ)$ for which every maximal left ideal is generated by $x_1-a_1,\ldots,x_n-a_n$, with $σ(a_j)a_i=σ(a_i)a_j$. The criterion consists of right $σ$-algebraic closure of $D$ and right algebraic closure of the centralizers of all commuting $(n-2)$-tuples in each twisted fixed division ring $E_a=\{c\in D:σ(c)a=ac\}$ for $0\ne a\in D$.

title: Nonradial threshold scattering for the planar cubic--quintic NLS
authors: Bo Yang, Lei Zhang, Bin Liu
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study the planar cubic--quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation \[ i\partial_tu+Δu=-|u|^2u+|u|^4u, \qquad (t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2, \] with initial data $u_0\in H^1_x(\mathbb R^2)$. We prove scattering in both time directions when the mass of \(u_0\) equals the mass of the ground state for the focusing cubic equation. This resolves the nonradial threshold scattering problem posed by Murphy [\emph{Comm.\ Partial Differential Equations} \textbf{46} (2021), 2213--2234]. Together with the known subthreshold scattering theory and the existence of standing waves at every larger mass, this identifies the sharp mass range in which every $H^1$ solution scatters. The proof combines localized interaction Morawetz estimates with propagation estimates on moving halfspaces to control exterior kinetic energy.

title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners
authors: Gaoxiang Linghu, Haonan Zhou, Xuanhe Liu, Weili Xu, Kaiyue Zhou, Jun Xiao, Gaoang Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.

title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
authors: Hui Chen, Haoyu Liu, Ke Wu, Dexin Zhou
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study whether visually similar price histories predict similar future returns, using a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar charts from three decades of U.S. price histories. A representation pretrained only on natural images already retrieves neighbors whose realized returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Aligning the representation with subsequent returns more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio and outperforms a convolutional neural network trained directly on chart images. The predictability is concentrated among stocks with greater limits to arbitrage. Returns and order imbalances around portfolio formation indicate that the signal identifies temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. A sparse autoencoder traces the return-aligned signal to recurring visual states that determine which historical charts are retrieved. Our approach traces each forecast to dated historical charts, making it more transparent than direct image-to-return models and linking rule-based technical analysis with machine-learning chart reading.

title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
authors: Mengran Li, Xichen Yan, Bo Li, Chengyang Zhang, Jinfeng Xu, Zheng Lin, Zelin Zang, Zhen Lei, Jiebo Luo, Victor C. M. Leung, Stan Z. Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Keke Tang, Guolin Qiu, Tianyu Hao, Daizong Liu, Yikai Zhang, Peican Zhu, Zhihong Tian
publish: arXiv
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.

title: Producing $μ$Bq/m3-level low-226Ra ultrapure water for the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory
authors: Xi-Ting Xu, Cong Guo, Jin-Chang Liu, Yong-Peng Zhang, Xiao-Hua Liang, Xin-Jian Wen, Chang-Gen Yang, Quan Tang, Li-Dan Lv, Yuan-Hao Niu, Bin Xiao
publish: arXiv
abstract: The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20 kton low-background liquid-scintillator (LS) detector, was designed primarily to determine the neutrino mass ordering. JUNO requires ultrapure water (UPW) with a Ra concentration < 50~$μ$Bq/m3 because of the direct liquid-liquid contact between LS and UPW during detector filling. To meet this stringent requirement, a high-sensitivity measurement system capable of detecting Ra in water down to 3.9 $μ$Bq/m3 was developed, and the 100 t/h UPW production process was optimized. By integrating selective ion-exchange resin with membrane-based separation technologies, the system consistently produced UPW with a Ra concentration of <4$μ$Bq/m3, exceeding the JUNO specification and, to our knowledge, representing one of the lowest reported levels achieved at this engineering scale. This paper describes the design and implementation of JUNO's UPW system and the high-sensitivity Ra measurement platform, together with a systematic evaluation of Ra removal efficiencies across the purification train and validation of the final water quality.

title: Fisher Information Characterization in GNSS DPE under Multipath-Induced Channel Uncertainty
authors: Sijia Li, Bing Xu, Shuo Tang, Pau Closas
publish: arXiv
abstract: The availability and utilization of Fisher information in global navigation satellite system (GNSS) direct position estimation (DPE) under multipath-induced channel uncertainty are investigated. First, a unified estimation-theoretic framework is developed to characterize information mapping and utilization across direct and two-step receivers. Next, a scalar-equivalent statistical channel model for short-delay multipath is established via least-squares (LS) projection. Based on this model, receiver-state Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs) are derived under perfect and statistical channel knowledge, while misspecified CRBs (MCRBs) are derived under a simplified deterministic complex-gain model that neglects channel uncertainty. The closed-form approximations and asymptotic analyses of the derived bounds further reveal how channel uncertainty affects different components of waveform-domain Fisher information. Our results reveal that: 1) DPE and fully coupled two-step estimation achieve comparable accuracy, whereas the performance loss caused by sequential decoupling substantially exceeds the additional loss from suboptimal weighting; 2) under statistical channel knowledge, improving received signal quality does not necessarily yield noticeable positioning gains; 3) positioning information remains available even as the coherent channel mean vanishes; and 4) neglecting channel randomness causes the MCRBs to diverge in this limit and can introduce positioning error floors that become more pronounced with longer observations.

title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
authors: Hung Dang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.

title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
authors: Yiming Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.

title: Two-Dimensional Ferromagnetic Weyl Half-Semimetal
authors: Yu-Yang Zhao, Chen-Hao Lv, Qing-Bo Liu, Wen-Neng Zhao, Xin-Yi Chen, Lun Xiong
publish: arXiv
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic topological materials provide appealing platforms for realizing spin-polarized topological states, yet the coexistence of Weyl fermions and robust high-temperature ferromagnetism remains elusive. Here, based on first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations, we predict monolayer BaMn$_4$O$_8$ to be a dynamically, thermally, and mechanically stable ferromagnetic Weyl half-semimetal. \textcolor{blue}{An anisotropic Monte Carlo simulation on a $20\times20\times1$ lattice yields a finite-size transition estimate of approximately 1446~K.} The spin-resolved electronic structure reveals a fully spin-polarized state, in which the spin-up channel hosts linear Weyl band crossings near the Fermi level, whereas the spin-down channel remains insulating. Corresponding Fermi-arc edge states connecting the projected Weyl points (WPs) are clearly observed along the (100) boundary, confirming the nontrivial topology. Importantly, both the Weyl points and their associated Fermi arcs remain robust in the presence of spin--orbit coupling (SOC). \textcolor{blue}{These results identify monolayer BaMn$_4$O$_8$ as a candidate for fully spin-polarized topological transport.

title: Extremal Projectors and the Virasoro Algebra
authors: Jonas T. Hartwig, Sagar Shrivastava
publish: arXiv
abstract: Extremal projectors are universal operators projecting onto the highest weight space in a representation. Their existence and uniqueness (as formal series) are known for a broad range of Lie superalgebras and quantum groups. We consider a class of Lie superalgebras that contains reductive finite-dimensional Lie algebras as well as the Virasoro algebra. We prove the existence and uniqueness of an extremal projector for this class. The existence proof is given in terms of a recursive algorithm which can be used to compute the coefficients. To illustrate the method, we compute the terms for the Virasoro extremal projector up to order 6. Furthermore, we formulate a conjecture for the denominators of the truncated extremal projector of the Virasoro algebra. We provide symbolic computational evidence up to order 6 and prove a weaker version of the conjecture.

title: Connectivity of Matroids with Breadth-Critical Tangles
authors: Zhuo Li, Zhen Chen
publish: arXiv
abstract: We construct an explicit infinite sequence of nonnegative integers $(s_0,s_1,\ldots)$ such that, for every $k\ge2$, every finite matroid with a breadth-critical tangle of order at least $k$ is $(s_0,s_1,\ldots,s_{k-2})$-connected. The constants $s_i$ depend only on $i$. This proves a conjecture of Brettell, Jowett, Oxley, Semple, and Whittle.

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
authors: Johannes Mootz, Mani Amani, Reza Akhavian
publish: arXiv
abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
authors: Kevin Rojas, Felix X. -F. Ye, Molei Tao
publish: arXiv
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
authors: Artur Kuramshin, Charlotte Cloutier, Michael Przystupa, Kirsty Ellis, Mohammad S. Akhter, Glen Berseth
publish: arXiv
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

title: Image-Condition-Controlled Diffusion Network with Large-Scale CT Pretraining for CT-Free Attenuation Correction in Dynamic Cardiac PET
authors: Zhejia Zhang, Scott M. Leonard, Jinkui Hao, Ryan J. Avery, Richard L. Weinberg, Bo Zhou
publish: arXiv
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) provides quantitative information on myocardial perfusion. In dynamic PET, tracer kinetics are tracked through a series of reconstructed time frames. Reliable attenuation correction is essential for accurate measurements. Clinical attenuation maps ($μ$-maps) are typically derived from computed tomography (CT), which adds radiation exposure and may introduce PET-CT misregistration due to respiratory and cardiac motion. Moreover, supervised CT-free methods rely on paired non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET and CT data, which are scarce, whereas large-scale unpaired CT data are more readily available. To address these challenges, we propose Large-scale Unpaired CT-Informed Diffusion (LUCID), a framework that transfers anatomical priors learned from 10,000 chest CT volumes in the public CT-RATE dataset to $μ$-map synthesis for dynamic cardiac $^{82}$Rb PET. First, a convolutional neural network (CNN) predicts an initial $μ$-map from each NAC PET frame. Second, the CT-pretrained diffusion backbone refines a low-noise perturbation of the CNN prediction through a single denoising step, conditioned on the corresponding NAC PET frame via ControlNet. Finally, frame-wise predictions are averaged voxel-wise to obtain the final $μ$-map. We further introduce the voxel-wise temporal standard deviation (TSD) to quantify inter-frame variability without requiring a reference $μ$-map. We evaluated LUCID on an in-house dataset of 102 patients and found that it achieved the best quantitative accuracy while maintaining competitive inter-frame consistency. Ablation studies showed that refinement with a diffusion backbone pretrained on in-house CT data from the training patients was less accurate than the CNN prediction alone, highlighting the importance of large-scale CT pretraining.

title: EyeDiT: Anatomy-Grounded Multi-Modal Eye Generation and Simulation
authors: Yonghan Lee, Zachary Willms, Kun Liu, Pushkar Anand, Ali Behrooz, Dmitri Model, Dinesh Manocha, Yatong An
publish: arXiv
abstract: Synthetic eye data are critical for rapid development of eye tracking (ET) in AR/VR applications. However, existing synthetic eye generators are largely image-centric and lack a high-quality underlying 3D anatomy of the eye, which limits their control mainly to the gaze and provides no anatomical labels. To address this problem, we propose EyeDiT, an anatomy-grounded, multi-modal 3D eye generation and simulation model trained with optical coherence tomography (OCT), labeled anatomy point clouds and near-eye images. Our pipeline first trains a Multi-Modal Anatomy Variational Autoencoder (VAE), which encodes an anatomy-aware latent representation from all input modalities. Then, our Eye Latent DiT is trained to generate latent samples conditioned on the optical axis, the pupil position and radius, and the subject identity. Together with Gaussian decoders for novel-view simulation, our model enables control over the pupil, subject identity and viewpoint for data synthesis. We show that our model outperforms previous eye image synthesis models in novel-view synthesis (24.9 against 21.8 dB PSNR from a single view), and that a public ET neural network trained on our synthetic data shows a smaller sim-to-real gap than when trained on data from other generators (3.5$^\circ$ vs. 8.4$^\circ$ gaze error), approaches a network trained on real data, and further improves ET performance when combined with real data (2.3$^\circ$ vs. 2.6$^\circ$). More information is available on the project page: https://lyhan12.github.io/eyedit

title: Circular decompositions for hyperbolic genus one knots
authors: Mario Eudae-Muñoz, Araceli Guzmán-Tristán, Fabiola Manjarrez-Gutiérrez, Enrique Ramírez-Losada
publish: arXiv
abstract: We consider hyperbolic genus one knots having two or more non-isotopic, disjoint, genus one Seifert surfaces, with the property that the complementary regiones are handlebody pairs. We determine whether or not these knots have circular width equal to $(3)$. Moreover we give bounds on their circular widths. We also give explicit examples of such knots having three or five non-isotopic genus one Seifert surfaces and compute their circular widths. In particular this shows that many of these knots are non-almost fibered.

title: Conditional limit theorems in dynamical systems
authors: Jason Atnip, Gary Froyland, Cecilia González-Tokman, Yushi Nakano, Sandro Vaienti
publish: arXiv
abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theory of conditional limit theorems for open dynamical systems. We study the statistical properties of the dynamics within transient regimes by establishing a suite of limit theorems describing the behavior of trajectories under the condition that they remain outside a ``hole'', or region of no return. Under a spectral gap assumption for the associated open transfer operator, we first establish conditioning and Yaglom limits and identify the corresponding conditionally invariant and conditionally ergodic measures. We then establish conditional exponential decay of correlations and the Strong Law of Large Numbers for both deterministic and quenched random systems. We also obtain a conditional Central Limit Theorem, Large Deviation Principle, and Berry--Esseen theorem, with additional assumptions in the quenched random case. We also derive standard (non-conditional) limit theorems on the surviving set of points that never enter the hole.

title: Theorems of the Alternative and Nonnegativity Certificates for Systems of Jensen-type Polynomials with Universal Quantifiers
authors: Feng Guo, Yuhang Guo, Guoyin Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: We introduce Jensen-type polynomials, a class of possibly nonconvex polynomials that extends the Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials while retaining natural sums of squares (SOS) certificates for nonnegativity. We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.

title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
authors: Advith Natarajan, Xinyang Zhou, Guido Cavraro
publish: arXiv
abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
authors: Zeman Li, Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Praneeth Kacham, Rami Al-Rfou, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni
publish: arXiv
abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

title: Removable forests in $k$-connected and $k$-edge-connected graphs
authors: Xu Liu, Bo Ning
publish: arXiv
abstract: We prove the forest conjecture of Clay and Jordán: Let $k\ge1$ be an integer and let $F$ be a forest with $m$ vertices and $e$ edges. If a $k$-connected graph $G$ has minimum degree at least $\max\{k+e,m-1\}$, then it contains a copy of $F$ whose edge deletion preserves $k$-connectivity. We also prove the $k$-edge-connectivity version.

title: Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
authors: Alexander Shapiro, Yan Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
authors: Jennifer Zhang, Amanda Coston
publish: arXiv
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
authors: Rafsan Jany, Md Rafid Islam, Mohammad Fahim Islam, Hafiz Abdur Rahman
publish: arXiv
abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
authors: Ghadi Nehme, Dahyun Nam, Akshay Govind Srinivasan, Faez Ahmed
publish: arXiv
abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

title: Match Rate Is Not Match Quality
authors: Tobias B. Konitzer, David M. Rothschild
publish: arXiv
abstract: Third-party identity-resolution vendors commonly emphasize match rate, the share of submitted records they can link to identifiers for advertising activation, as their core metric of quality. Yet a high match rate does not necessarily mean that those matched identifiers belong to the submitted records (i.e., the intended targets). In this paper we explore match quality as an alternative metric to match rate, utilizing a unique data set to evaluate match quality. We are able to compare two demographics, age and gender, from a submitted record (voter files) to the same demographics in self-reported surveys matched to mobile advertising identifiers linked together by two leading identity-resolution vendors. The data and matching was from 2019-20. There is substantial ambiguity in match quality of the returned records. First, both vendors' activation files contain multiple device identifiers per match. Second, match quality among audited pairs (Vendor A) and for explicitly labeled individual-level matches (Vendor B) is only 21.8% and 23.6%, respectively. Utilizing a mixture model that assumes that correct links always agree on these two demographics and incorrect links agree 10% of the time, these rates imply conditional identity-level precisions of approximately 15% and 13%, respectively. This paper utilizes identity-resolution products that are several years old, but the question we address remains fundamental: match rate alone cannot establish whether advertisers are reaching the people they intended. Evaluating identity resolution requires independent evidence of match quality alongside match rate.

title: Implementation of LDA+Gutzwiller with Newton's method
authors: Jian Zhang, Ming-Feng Tian, Guang-Xi Jin, Yuan-Feng Xu, Xi Dai
publish: arXiv
abstract: In order to calculate the electronic structure of correlated materials, we propose implementation of the LDA+Gutzwiller method with Newton's method. The self-consistence process, efficiency and convergence of calculation are improved dramatically by using Newton's method with golden section search and other improvement approaches. We compare the calculated results by applying the previous linear mix method and Newton's method. We have applied our code to study the electronic structure of several typical strong correlated materials, including SrVO$_3$, LaCoO$_3$, and La$_2$O$_3$Fe$_2$Se$_2$. Our results fit quite well with the previous studies.

title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
authors: Chanhwi Jeong, Dongmin You, Seungwook Kim
publish: arXiv
abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

title: Re-Testing LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translations Against Their Original C
authors: Muhammad Hassnain
publish: arXiv
abstract: Most C-to-Rust translators use large language models (LLMs), and each reports a success rate from its own correctness check. We survey 34 C-to-Rust translators that use LLMs. Only one reports testing its check, and eleven release the original C and their Rust in runnable form. We re-test all eleven. We run the C and the Rust on generated inputs, compare every output, and count a divergence only where the C has no undefined behavior. All eleven release defective translations: we find 160 defects, 93 of them outright errors on ordinary inputs. Their own checks accepted 86 defective translations. For 81 of them, the released check never compared the programs on an input that exposes the defect. For three of the other five, it ran one but compared only part of the output. A success rate is only as good as its check. Before counting a translation as a success, authors should compare every output with the C's on inputs the repair loop never saw, check that a verifier reaches its assertion, release exactly what the check accepted, and report how they tested the check.

title: Bernstein-Zelevinsky duality for equivariant vector bundles on Drinfeld spaces
authors: Zhenghui Li, Benchao Su, Zhixiang Wu
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study duality and finiteness of locally analytic representations arising from compactly supported coherent cohomology of Drinfeld spaces. We prove that Grothendieck--Serre duality for equivariant vector bundles realizes Bernstein--Zelevinsky duality of locally analytic representations. We follow the strategy of Fargues for $\ell$-adic sheaves and obtain resolutions of locally analytic representations by compactly induced representations. The resolutions motivate us to introduce the notion of locally analytic representations of compact presentation, which generalizes the notion of finitely presented representations. These representations are related to prim objects on the classifying stack in the sense of $6$-functor formalism and their extension groups to admissible locally analytic representations are finite-dimensional. As an application, we establish Serre duality for extension groups of locally analytic representations of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ attached to non-trianguline de Rham Galois representations under the $p$-adic local Langlands correspondence.

title: Euler-Lagrange Equations Formulated in Terms of Angular Velocity
authors: Katsutoshi Yoshida
publish: arXiv
abstract: We propose a novel variant of the Euler--Lagrange (EL) equation for rigid body rotation, explicitly formulated in terms of orientation parameters $\thh$ and angular velocity $\omm$. Variational analysis of the stationarity condition of the action integral for a Lagrangian in terms of $\thh$ and $\omm$ yields a modified EL formulation. For pure rotational motion, the proposed equation directly recovers equations of motion fully consistent with the classical Euler equations, bypassing explicit geometry-based torque analysis. Furthermore, the framework seamlessly accommodates coupled translational and rotational dynamics, as validated through a spring-suspended symmetrical top, exhibiting exact agreement with the Newton--Euler equations. We also identify an inherent discrepancy in the standard EL approach, demonstrating that applying a direct coordinate transformation $\dot\thh\mapsto\omm$ causes the resulting formulation to deviate from both the classical Euler equation and our proposed formulation. The proposed framework is expected to provide an intuitive, versatile modeling tool for spatial rigid body dynamics.

title: Slice Isolation-as-a-Service: An Isolation Mechanism to Proactively Defend Cross-Slice Attacks in 5G-Advanced and Beyond
authors: Abdulaziz Abdulghaffar, Ashraf Matrawy
publish: arXiv
abstract: As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. Empirical evaluations under active volumetric flooding and the recently discovered GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks reveal that shared and Virtualized Network Function (VNF)-only isolation fail catastrophically, suffering up to 30% packet loss and complete bandwidth starvation. Our results prove that MINLP-driven strict physical isolation successfully neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability for mission-critical slices, confirming our isolation framework as a crucial proactive defense for next-generation core networks.

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
authors: Wen Wang, Jindong Wang, Jiahua Bao, Tu Yongsiqi, Yihao Liu, Junwei He, Wenkui Fan
publish: arXiv
abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

title: Hurwitz equivalence in quandles of order at most four
authors: Takuto Hosoo, Kodai Wada
publish: arXiv
abstract: Let $X$ be a quandle and let $m\geq 2$ be an integer. The $m$-braid group acts on the $m$-fold Cartesian power $X^m$ by the Hurwitz action. For an $m$-tuple $\boldsymbol{x}\in X^m$, we introduce two invariants of the Hurwitz action: the product $Π(\boldsymbol{x})$ of its entries in the associated group $\operatorname{As}(X)$ and the orbit multiplicities $μ_w(\boldsymbol{x})$ $(w\in X)$. We prove that these two invariants completely classify Hurwitz equivalence classes for all quandles of order at most four. We also establish a complete classification of Hurwitz equivalence classes for a class of amalgamated sums of trivial quandles and a reduction theorem for disjoint sums with trivial quandles. Finally, we study the corresponding action of the virtual braid group. For this action, the orbit multiplicities alone give a complete classification for every quandle of order at most four.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
authors: Jinbae Seo, Jungin Park, Hyunsung Jang, Namkoo Ha, Jiyoung Lee, Kwanghoon Sohn
publish: arXiv
abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
authors: Hai Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
authors: He-Guang Xu, G. D. de Moraes Neto
publish: arXiv
abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.

title: The Population of Radio Hypernebulae from Mass-Transferring Massive Binaries
authors: Kohki Uno, Brian D. Metzger, Navin Sridhar, Lieke A. C. van Son, Floor S. Broekgaarden, Dillon Z. Dong, Keiichi Maeda
publish: arXiv
abstract: Massive binary evolution is punctuated by brief phases of highly super-Eddington mass transfer (MT) onto neutron stars and black holes, presaging luminous transients such as supernovae, common envelope events, and gravitational wave sources. These hyper-accreting phases power relativistic jets and slower mass-loaded outflows, inflating extended nebulae of relativistic particles. Though observed in the local universe as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries and micro-quasars, the present census is biased against shorter-lived and hence rarer but potentially even more extreme MT systems: so-called ``hypernebulae'' (HNbe). We use the binary population synthesis code (\textsc{COMPAS}) to estimate the MT population, which spans a wide range of MT rates $\dot{M} \sim 10^{2-7}\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$ and source lifetimes $t_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{0-6}$ years. Combining this synthetic population with a semi-analytic model for their time-dependent radio emission, we predict the observable properties of HNbe over cosmic time. HNbe exhibit a broad GHz luminosity range extending to $L_{ν, \rm peak} \sim 10^{28-30}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, and up to $\sim 10^{2}$ ($\sim 10^{5}$) HNbe are detectable by the wide-field radio surveys VLASS (DSA-2000) in our conservative model. A fraction of these systems should possess angular sizes and spatial offsets from star-forming regions (due to the first supernova kick) resolvable by VLBI. The most luminous donors, helium Hertzsprung-gap stars, may be detectable coincident with radio HNbe with Roman imaging out to distances $\sim 30$\,Mpc. Our findings suggest HNbe as promising probes of the pathways linking massive binaries to energetic transients.

title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
authors: Tianqi Chen
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $β\ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $β$-TEF1 allocation.

title: Subsequent Dust-Fading Events of the Wolf-Rayet Star WR 59: A Continuous Visual Record
authors: Rod Stubbings
publish: arXiv
abstract: This paper presents long-term visual and space-based monitoring of the WC9d Wolf-Rayet star WR 59 from 2017 to 2026, documenting a profound physical transition from a stable baseline to an ongoing phase of continuous dust production. Visual observations using a 22-inch telescope initially established a four-year quiescent baseline at magnitude 13.9. Following the historic May 2021 discovery fade to magnitude 15.2, long-term nightly visual monitoring documented an accelerating sequence of twelve distinct fading episodes over subsequent years, characterised by progressively shorter inter-fade recovery intervals. Due to severe pixel crowding and flux contamination from a close 11.7 V companion star 11 arcseconds away, automated large-pixel survey pipelines remain completely blind to these high-amplitude fading events. Direct comparisons with NASA's TESS satellite photometry during quiet phases show that targeted visual magnitude estimates measure systemic baseline micro-variations with professional accuracy while bridging space mission coverage gaps. High-density observation blocks during the minimum floor reveal a highly dynamic, rapid, minute-by-minute bimodal oscillation and sub-minute flickering between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2. At the time of writing, the system remains locked in an unprecedented deep minimum, varying between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2 for a sustained period exceeding 102 consecutive days. Intensive visual monitoring is ongoing to record the eventual egress recovery profile.

title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
authors: Yasuhiro Yoshimura, Toshiya Hanada
publish: arXiv
abstract: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.

title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
authors: Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Guanyu Zhu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-ε}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<ε<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $γ\rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-ε}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Jianhuan Mao, Mengxiao Zhu, Yue Pei, Lei Li, Haogang Zhu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.

title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
authors: Hong Jun Kim, Gun Sik Min, Seok-Hyung Lee, Jun Heo
publish: arXiv
abstract: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
authors: Ilia Karpov, Kirill Koloskov, Valeriy Kuleshov, Dmitry Ilvovsky
publish: arXiv
abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.

title: ACUS: An Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score for Incomplete-View CT
authors: Zihan Deng, Chuanzhi Xu, Quankeng Huang, Yujie Liu, Zhenzhen Gong, Junjie Huang, Tianye Niu, Lequan Yu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Sparse-view and limited-arc computed tomography (CT) are commonly treated as projection completion: a network fills an unmeasured view, and the result is ranked by similarity to one ground-truth image. That score can be high even when the query angle is far from every acquired measurement, because a learned prior may invent anatomy the scan never constrained. Existing protocols therefore leave a basic question unanswered: how does predictive reliability change with distance from the acquired views? We propose the Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score (ACUS) to answer that question. ACUS is the Winkler interval score of a nominal 90% predictive interval on held-out projections, binned by distance to the nearest acquired view. It charges interval width and adds a large miss penalty when a held-out pixel falls outside the interval, so a narrow band helps only when coverage holds. We use collapse on acquired angles as a necessary consistency check on the predictor. On chest and dental cone-beam orbits, interval width grows with the angular gap. Empirical coverage ranges from 77% to 92%, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the point estimate falls as the width rises. Nearest-neighbor, interpolation, and point completion, each given one residual scale, have zero reported far coverage and incur outside-distance penalties. ACUS exposes gap-dependent overconfidence that a point-estimate PSNR alone does not measure.

title: Some Results on the Complex Oscillation of Second-Order Linear Differential Equations
authors: Shi-Jian Wu, Jian-Tang Lu, Xiong-Feng Liu
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study the zeros of solutions of $f''+A(z)f=0$ with an entire coefficient $A$. We answer two questions of Gundersen affirmatively. We prove that if $A$ has finite order and the exponent of convergence of its distinct zeros is smaller than its order, then the zeros of the product of any two linearly independent solutions have infinite exponent of convergence. We also prove that if $A$ has finite order and the exponent of convergence of its zeros, counted with multiplicity, is smaller than its order, then the zeros of every non-trivial solution have infinite exponent of convergence.

title: Expressiveness and Convertibility of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
authors: Amir Masoumzadeh, Paliath Narendran, Padmavathi Iyer
publish: arXiv
abstract: Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.

title: Kernel Design in Particle Mesh Ewald Methods: Splitting, Interpolation, and Upsampling
authors: Shidong Jiang, Jiuyang Liang, Libin Lu
publish: arXiv
abstract: For more than thirty years, particle mesh Ewald (PME) methods have dominated the computation of electrostatic interactions in molecular dynamics. A PME method uses a splitting kernel to divide the interaction into a local part, summed within a cutoff, and a smooth part, computed on a grid with a spreading and interpolation (SI) kernel. The established methods use Ewald's Gaussian split with B-spline SI kernels, and the recent Ewald summation with prolates accelerates them severalfold by using a prolate spheroidal wave function (PSWF) for both kernels. Neither choice meets two needs of molecular dynamics: a smooth energy, which long simulations need in order to conserve it, and a low-order SI kernel that stays accurate on coarse grids and gains accuracy as the grid is refined. We present a framework for designing both kernels to meet these needs. For inverse powers from the Coulomb to the dispersion interaction, our splits make the local part smooth at the cutoff to any order while keeping the Fourier concentration of the smooth part close to optimal. We show that with analytic differentiation, the force error of a continuous SI kernel of fixed shape vanishes under grid refinement only if every particle, wherever it lies, gives the grid its exact charge and dipole moment. Our SI kernel for the Coulomb interaction ensures this by construction and is twice continuously differentiable. Compared with the B-spline of the same order, it needs fewer grid points by a factor of up to nearly five; on coarse grids, it mostly needs a lower order than the PSWF kernel. In simulations of liquid water over 100 million time steps, the new kernels reduce the energy drift of both the established and the PSWF kernels by about three orders of magnitude, with a smaller force error than either. Existing PME codes can adopt them by replacing only the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier.

title: A Complete Classification of the One-Dimensional Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problem
authors: Ziyi Chi, Fanze Kong, Juichen Wei
publish: arXiv
abstract: We give a complete classification of the spectral stability of the following one-dimensional nonlocal eigenvalue problem (NLEP) $$ \partial_x^2φ-φ+pw^{p-1}φ-γ(p-1)\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^{r-1}φdx}{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^r dx}w^p=λφ, $$ where $w$ is the unique positive even solution of $w''-w+w^p=0$ decaying at infinity, $p,r>1$, and $γ\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\Reγ\ge0$. This type of NLEP appears frequently in pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems. We show that on the even subspace, strict spectral stability holds exactly for $\Reγ>1$ when $r=(p+3)/2$. In the $γ$-plane, when $r>(p+3)/2$, two conjugate boundary arcs open to the left from $γ=1$, and the strictly stable region lies to their right. When $r<(p+3)/2$, the arcs open to the right, and the strictly stable region lies between them. Their common endpoint is $γ=1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $γ=γ_H>1$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$. In each case, the two arcs approach a common vertical asymptote. As an application, for real $γ\ge0$, the condition for strict spectral stability is $γ>1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $γ>γ_H$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$, where $γ_H>1$ is the value at which a conjugate pair of eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis. The key ingredient in determining how the number of eigenvalues in the open right half-plane changes at imaginary-axis crossings is a cumulative estimate for the mixed-sign spectral weights that arise for certain $p$ and $r$ with $1<p<3$ and $1<r<2$.

title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
authors: Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
publish: arXiv
abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise.
