The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
authors: Haoxuan Wang, Jianliang Ye, Sen Na
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

title: Wei-Norman Factorization of Frenet-Serret equations and the Cardan Lock
authors: Julio Guerrero, Rafael Florencio
publish: arXiv
abstract: Frenet-Serret equations for particles moving along differentiable curves, in the case of non-constant curvature and torsion, are considered in the framework of the Wei-Norman factorization of the propagator using the Lie algebra of the rotation group. It leads to a system of coupled linear equations that are highly coupled if Euler or Cardan angles are used, but that can be uncoupled if the Cartan basis in the Lie algebra is used, resulting essentially in a Ricatti equation. However, since the rotations algebra is not a solvable algebra, the global Wei-Norman Theorem does not apply and singularities in the solutions of the system of equations appear at certain points, related to the \text{gimbal o Cardan lock}. Notwidthstanding, a detailed study of the limit at these points shows that in most of the cases the propagator is well defined and gimbal lock is avoided.

title: From Persistent Cohomology to Maps into Arbitrary Eilenberg-MacLane Spaces
authors: Tony Xiaochen Xiao, Jose A. Perea
publish: arXiv
abstract: In this paper, we address the construction of Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates (functions from datasets to Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $K(G,n)$) that encode nontrivial persistent cohomology classes in arbitrary dimensions $n$ and coefficient group $G$. The construction leverages the connecting homomorphism in the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology, from the short exact sequence of sheaves of continuous maps with values in $G$, $EG$ and $BG$. Crucially, the derivation is constructive: we give an explicit, recursive formula for preimages under the connecting homomorphism, which yields a constructive version of a classical cohomology vanishing theorem and, in turn, an algorithm for general Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates. We validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets, and present novel examples of $K(\mathbb{Z}/2, 2)$-coordinates not addressed in prior work.

title: A Tail-Geometric Approach to Kotlarski's Lemma with Order Statistics
authors: Yao Luo
publish: arXiv
abstract: We develop a tail-geometric approach to nonparametric identification in repeated-measurement models based on large within-unit gaps. Differencing eliminates the common latent component, while conditioning on a large gap pushes the idiosyncratic errors into opposite tails. Under a regular thinner-than-Gaussian tail condition, an idiosyncratic component concentrates around a deterministic, gap-dependent location. Consequently, the corresponding observed measurement, after recentering, reveals the distribution of the common latent component up to location. The idiosyncratic distribution can then be recovered through deconvolution. This principle applies both to the classical two-measurement Kotlarski model and to settings where only order statistics are observed. Applications include auctions and wage-offer models, whether all offers are observed or only the top-ranked ones are available.

title: SADIC: Improving Protein Atom Depth Computation Using Morphological Transformations_supp1-3753758.pdf
authors: Giacomo Nunziati
publish: N/A
abstract: Structural analysis is fundamental to understanding the biological function of proteins. Among structural descriptors, atomic depth plays a key role in identifying folding motifs, assessing stability, and characterising molecular interactions. A prior method for computing atomic depth, implemented in the Simple Atom Depth Index Calculator (SADIC), leveraged Discrete Geometry to capture local molecular shape. In this work, we present a novel approach that integrates Discrete Geometry and Mathematical Morphology to compute volume-based atom depth indices using a digital-space representation of macromolecular structures. A core feature of the method is a morphological strategy for detecting solvent-inaccessible cavities, enabling their inclusion in volume computation without altering the protein's overall three-dimensional structure. The approach supports solvent-specific probing of cavity accessibility and provides a balanced characterisation of deeply buried atoms while preserving the high variability of superficial atom depths, a hallmark of volume-based descriptors. Computational efficiency is further enhanced by introducing a translated reference sphere for depth calculation. We evaluate the method on a dataset of 1000 proteins with diverse sizes and shapes, demonstrating greater effectiveness, reduced estimated protein volume, and significantly faster execution times compared to existing approaches. Additionally, the depth indices agree closely with those computed by the DEPTH algorithm, but offer a finer-grained characterisation of superficial atoms.
